title: Maps That Age
thesis: Maps do not simply become old: printing plates accumulate repairs, recut borders and altered names, while later states preserve inherited geometries that make political change look continuous. Reading successive states exposes age as an editorial process rather than a date.
whyThisSite: Terra Chartarum can place dated states of the same plate in a CompareSlider, record state-specific changes in the catalogue and expose a filterable state ledger, making revision visible without pretending that every difference is a new map.

claims.claim: The Theatrum was repeatedly revised across thirty-one editions and seven languages between 1570 and 1612.
The first world-map plate accumulated hachuring changes, repair marks, a partly mended crack, fading linework and added dates across six documented states.
The short-lived second plate moved through three states, including removal of its date and correction of the South American coastline.
The third plate replaced the earlier plates and was itself altered after 1613 by adding Le Maire Strait and changing the surrounding hachuring.
Close plate comparison can reveal differences missed when similar maps are inspected in alternation rather than superimposed.
Ortelius’s world map also functioned as a philosophical and emblematic image, so revision preserved a visual argument as well as geography.
